text: Time to turn the plan from last lesson into real T-SQL. Everything here against AdventureWorks2012 — nothing invented, nothing that should surprise you if you followed the plan.

The FROM and JOIN block matches the plan exactly. Start at SalesOrderDetail, aliased sod. Join up to SalesOrderHeader, aliased soh, on SalesOrderID. Join sideways to Product, aliased p, on ProductID. Join from the header's territory ID over to SalesTerritory, aliased st, on TerritoryID. Four tables, three join keys, same as the sketch.

The current-quarter filter builds its own date range instead of hardcoding one. DatePart quarter of GetDate gives today's quarter number, one through four. That gets converted into the quarter's starting month, and DateFromParts assembles day one of that month. The upper bound adds three months to that same date. The result is a half-open range — on or after the quarter starts, strictly before the next one does — so it never double-counts a boundary date, and it rolls forward automatically every quarter with zero edits.

The select list has the two grouping columns, territory name and product line, plus sum of line total for total sales amount, and count distinct sales order id for order count. Group by territory name and product line matches those two non-aggregated columns, exactly the GROUP BY rule you already know.

Why distinct, and not just count star? Because joining to SalesOrderDetail repeats each order's ID once per line item on that order. An order with three products produces three rows here. Count star would count line items — three — when the real order count is one. Count distinct sales order id counts the unique order, giving the correct number.
That's a complete, correct extract query, ready to run against AdventureWorks2012. Next lesson, we bring its results into Power BI and start shaping them in Power Query.
